newsitem.title: USA: U.S. renews vow to keep sanctions on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. renews vow to keep sanctions on Iraq.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday renewed its vow to use its veto to block the lifting of U.N. sanctions on Iraq as long as Baghdad impedes U.N. inspections of weapons of mass destruction.

"As long as this continues -- and it's continued now for seven years -- as long as it continues, the Iraqis have no hope of getting the U.N. sanctions lifted," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"We're on the Security Council. We have a veto in the Security Council. We will not let those sanctions be lifted until Iraq gives up its attempts to hide its weapons of mass destruction programmes," he said.

Burns was reacting to U.N. charges that Iraq obstructed flights by U.N. helicopters over its territory. Baghdad denied the charge. But Burns said the United States accepted the U.N. version of events.
Chief U.N. arms monitor Rolf Ekeus complained to the Security Council about Iraqi interference with U.N. helicopter flights during the inspection of several Iraqi facilities last week.

Ekeus, who heads the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, told the council in a letter that four serious incidents took place in the past few days to endanger U.N. crews.

He said Iraqi air personnel accompanying the flights once threatened to shut off the helicopter's fuel pump and physically manhandled the U.N. chief air inspector and the U.N. commission's photographer to prevent them from taking photographs of the inspection site.

In another incident the Iraqi personnel grabbed the co-pilot's control stick, resulting in the abortion of the mission. In the other two incidents an accompanying Iraqi helicopter placed itself in the path of the U.N. aircraft, forcing it to take radical evasive action.
Burns said with these incidents "the bizarre nature of the Iraqi regime has probably reached new heights."
The Iraqis "are putting the lives of the UNSCOM experts, as well as their own lives, into danger because they don't want to open up their country to UN observation," he said.
The Australian official who will soon replace Ekeaus in the U.N. job "is not going to put up with this nonsense from the Iraqis. And he will have the full support of the United States," Burns said.
He added: "But I mean, can you imagine this kind of behaviour? You probably can, from Saddam Hussein."
